card: Paper card. Question: How can high-entropy materials (HEMs) leverage configurational entropy to overcome the limitations of conventional enthalpy-dominated catalysts, specifically regarding phase stability, active site tunability, and the breaking of scaling relationships in electrocatalysis?. System: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) including PtPdCoNiFeCuAuSn, PtPdRhRuCe, Ru0.44Rh0.30Co0.12Ni0.14, CoxMoyFe10Ni10Cu10, IrPdPtRhRu, Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni, and AlNiCoIrM; High-entropy oxides (HEOs) and perovskites; Multimetallic nanoclusters (MMNCs).. Processing: Carbothermal shock (ultrafast joule heating followed by rapid quenching at ~1500 K); Fast moving bed pyrolysis (FMBP) reaching 923 K within 5 s; Colloidal synthesis with seed-mediated coreduction and annealing at 600°C; Ionic liquid-assisted cosputtering; Ball milling and solvothermal synthesis.. Test conditions: Ammonia oxidation at 700°C; Ammonia decomposition at 500°C; Oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) in acidic and alkaline media; Oxygen evolution reaction (OER) in acidic and alkaline media; Hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) in acidic and alkaline solutions; Li-O2 battery cycling.. Findings: Quinary HEA nanoparticles (PtPdRhRuCe) achieved ~100% conversion and >99% selectivity toward NO + NO2 at 700°C with no degradation over 30 hours.; HEA-Co25Mo45 catalyst reached a mass-specific rate of 0.74 gNH3 m−2 hour−1 at 500°C, representing improvement factors of ~24 versus bimetallic Co-Mo and ~19 versus Ru.; Computational models predicted an IrPdPtRhRu HEA composition with a ~40-mV lower overpotential relative to Pt (111) for ORR.; Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni nanoparticles with size less than 2 nm delivered ORR activity comparable to Pt under the same conditions.; Octonary RuIrCeNiWCuCrCo catalyst outperformed quaternary and binary counterparts in long-term operation for Li-O2 batteries due to higher configurational entropy.; GO-supported quinary HEA nanoparticles (FeCoPdIrPt) exhibited enhanced HER activity and stability in alkaline solutions relative to commercial Pt/C catalysts.; HEA catalysts containing five or more elements outperformed binary, ternary, and quaternary alloys in alkaline media due to broad adsorption energy distributions.. Mechanism: Enhanced configurational entropy stabilizes single-phase solid solutions despite large enthalpic differences, allowing atomic mixing of multiple principal elements. Severe lattice distortion lowers the energy barrier for adsorption and activation, while the diverse local coordination environments and electronic perturbations (ligand effects) create a near-continuum distribution of adsorption energies. This distribution allows the catalyst to access optimal binding strengths for intermediates, breaking the linear scaling relationships that limit conventional catalysts.. Limitations: Low surface area of bulk HEAs limits catalytic utilization; maintaining nanoscale morphology at elevated temperatures is difficult due to migration and aggregation; synthesis of single-phase HEAs requires overcoming thermodynamic barriers; characterization is challenging due to increased compositional and structural complexities; phase segregation can occur if entropy is insufficient to overcome enthalpic differences.. Future work: Further elucidation of structure-property relationships across different HEM subcategories; development of high-throughput synthesis and measurement tools for accelerated materials discovery; deeper mechanistic studies on surface restructuring under reaction conditions; optimization of catalyst stability for noble metal-free applications.. Quote: "The ability to confine multiple principal elements in a single lattice is intriguing for the design of advanced catalysts with desirable activity, selectivity, and stability."

Paper card. Question: How can the configurational entropy in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) be leveraged to overcome the miscibility limitations of traditional alloys and enhance catalytic performance for complex reactions like ethanol oxidation?. System: Platinum-group metal (PGM) high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles containing Ru, Rh, Pd, Os, Ir, and Pt; specifically compared against physical mixtures of unary PGMs and binary/ternary/quaternary/quinary PGM alloys.. Processing: Prepared using a facile polyol method to synthesize PGM-HEA nanoparticles.. Test conditions: Electrochemical ethanol oxidation reaction in aqueous solution; performance compared against commercial Pd/C, Pd black, Pt/C, and Au@PtIr/C catalysts; cyclic voltammetry used to analyze individual constituent contributions.. Findings: The PGM-HEA nanoparticles exhibited much higher activity relative to commercial Pd/C, Pd black, and Pt/C catalysts.; Negligible activity was observed for the physical mixture of the six unary PGM nanoparticles, confirming the necessity of atomic mixing.; The PGM-HEA delivered a mass activity more than 1.5 times higher than that of the most active catalyst to date (Au@PtIr/C).; The PGM-HEA exhibited the highest current density in the full potential range compared to ternary, quaternary, and quinary PGM alloys.; Pt and Pd are active for ethanol conversion but become poisoned by adsorbed (CO)ad or CHx species.; Os and Ru facilitate the oxidation of (CO)ad, mitigating the poisoning effect for Pt and Pd.; Ir and Ru ensure that dehydrogenation or C─C cleavage occurs at a low potential, while further oxidation hinges on Pt and Pd components.. Mechanism: The atomically mixed metals in HEAs play distinct yet concerted functions: Pt and Pd drive ethanol conversion; Os and Ru mitigate poisoning by oxidizing adsorbed species; Ir and Ru lower the potential for C─C cleavage and dehydrogenation. This synergy allows for efficient and complete oxidation of ethanol involving multiple proton-electron transfers.. Limitations: The text notes that while simple reactions can be triggered by mono- and bimetallic PGMs, it is difficult to drive complex reactions involving multiple proton-electron transfers and intermediate species without the synergistic effects provided by HEAs.. Future work: The authors imply the need to better understand the contribution of each metal to the overall reaction, as demonstrated by their comparison of cyclic voltammetry curves of individual constituents to elucidate specific roles in preventing poisoning and facilitating cleavage.. Quote: "The PGM-HEA nanoparticles efficiently catalyzed the ethanol oxidation reaction, exhibiting a much higher activity relative to that of the commercial Pd/C, Pd black, and Pt/C catalysts, respectively."

card: Paper card. Question: Can configurational entropy be engineered to stabilize a single-phase solid solution in a five-component oxide system where the constituent binary oxides do not form solid solutions, and can this transition be reversed?. System: Equimolar mixture of MgO, CoO, NiO, CuO, and ZnO (labeled E1). Processing: Solid-state synthesis: powders milled for 2 h, pressed into pellets at 31,000 N, fired in air at temperatures ranging from 700 to 1,100 °C with 50 °C increments, and quenched; thin films prepared via pulsed laser deposition at 600 °C with 3 J cm⁻² energy density.. Test conditions: X-ray diffraction (XRD) monitoring phase evolution from 700 to 1,100 °C; differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and in situ XRD at 5 °C min⁻¹; EXAFS at Advanced Photon Source 12-BM-B; STEM-EDS analysis at 200 kV.. Findings: Full conversion to a single-phase rocksalt structure occurs between 850 and 900 °C, with no additional peaks observed above this range.; Removing any single component from the five-component mixture results in a multiphase material when equilibrated at 875 °C for 12 h.; Deviations from equimolarity by ±2, ±6, and ±10% increase the transition temperature to single phase, confirming the entropic driving force.; The phase transformation from multiphase to single phase is endothermic, with a measured enthalpy change of approximately 12 kJ mol⁻¹ (±2 kJ mol⁻¹).; EXAFS data shows cation-to-anion first-neighbour distances are identical within ±0.01 Å for Zn, Ni, Cu, and Co, consistent with random distribution.; STEM-EDS mapping reveals chemically and structurally homogeneous material with no evidence of phase separation or clustering at the atomic scale.; A small mass loss of approximately 1.5% occurs at the transition due to the reduction of 3+ to 2+ cations during the conversion of spinel intermediates to rocksalt.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the high configurational entropy of the five-component equimolar mixture overcomes the positive enthalpic penalties associated with structural transitions (specifically for CuO and ZnO) and mixing, stabilizing the single-phase solid solution at elevated temperatures. The entropy term (TΔS) in the Gibbs free energy becomes dominant, driving the reversible transition from a multiphase state to a random solid solution where cations occupy a single sublattice homogeneously.. Limitations: The authors note that quantitative calorimetry presents challenges, and the assumption of ideal mixing for enthalpy calculations is a simplification; literature reports indicate finite and mixed-sign enthalpies of mixing that are not fully captured by the reference transition enthalpy values.. Future work: The authors propose that entropic stabilization should be explored in other systems with intermediate anions, such as chalcogenides, nitrides, and halides, particularly where covalent character is modest, and call for rigorous theoretical exploration of the crystallographic model where intermediate anions render cation sites energetically equivalent.. Quote: "entropy predominates the thermodynamic landscape, and drives a reversible solid-state transformation between a multiphase and single-phase state."

card: Paper card. Question: Is polymorphism still possible in entropy-stabilized high-entropy alloys (HEAs) that are generally believed to possess extremely high structural stability and maintain a single-phase structure?. System: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (Cantor's alloy). Processing: Synthesized via gas-atomization (melt injected into high purity Ar at 4 MPa pressure); subjected to hydrostatic compression up to ~41 GPa using a diamond anvil cell (DAC) with helium as pressure-transmitting medium; subsequently heated using resistive heating (up to 723 K) or double-sided Nd:YLF laser heating (up to ~1,400 K) at various pressures (6, 14, 26 GPa).. Test conditions: Room temperature compression up to ~41 GPa; heating at ambient pressure up to 723 K; heating at 6, 14, and 26 GPa up to ~1,400 K; in situ synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction (XRD) monitoring.. Findings: The fcc-to-hcp polymorphic transition starts at approximately 22 GPa and almost completes at approximately 41 GPa.; The phase transition is irreversible; the hcp phase is retained when pressure is released to ambient conditions.; The hcp phase remains stable up to 633 K at ambient pressure before transforming back to fcc.; At 26 GPa, the critical temperature for the hcp-to-fcc transition is approximately 1,400 K.; The isothermal bulk modulus (B0) is 153.9±3.0 GPa for the fcc phase and 150.2±4.6 GPa for the hcp phase.; The c/a ratio of the hcp phase remained almost constant at 1.62±0.01 during compression and decompression.; The transition is sluggish, with fcc and hcp phases coexisting over a wide pressure range of ~22 to ~41 GPa.; Decompression from different maximum pressures yields fcc/hcp composites with tunable fractions.. Mechanism: The transition occurs because the hcp structure is thermodynamically more favorable at lower temperatures and high pressures, while the fcc phase is stable at higher temperatures and lower pressures; the transition is kinetically hindered by high energy barriers and low stacking fault energy (~20 mJ m−2), requiring high pressure to overcome these barriers to form the hcp phase.. Limitations: The transition is sluggish and irreversible, making it difficult to determine the real equilibrium phase boundary (Clapeyron coexistence curve) experimentally; grain size was not small enough for statistically reliable Rietveld refinement of volume fractions; overshooting often exists due to high energy barriers.. Future work: The authors suggest that this behavior could be general in various HEAs and propose new avenues for tailoring HEA properties via polymorphic transition-induced HEA composites, particularly at cryogenic temperatures where transition pressure could be largely decreased.. Quote: "The transition is irreversible, and our in situ high-temperature synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction experiments at different pressures of the retained hcp high-entropy alloy reveal that the fcc phase is a stable polymorph at high temperatures, while the hcp structure is more thermodynamically favourable at lower temperatures."

W2909236073.title: High-Entropy Alloys as a Discovery Platform for Electrocatalysis

card: Paper card. Question: How can the miscibility gap in bimetallic Co-Mo alloys be overcome to create tunable, highly active catalysts for ammonia decomposition using earth-abundant elements?. System: Quinary CoMoFeNiCu high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (general composition CoxMoyFe10Ni10Cu10 where x + y = 70) and control samples of bimetallic Co-Mo and monometallic Ru. Processing: Carbothermal shock technique involving flash heating and cooling of metal precursors on oxygenated carbon nanofibers; temperature reached 2000–2300 K with ramping rates on the order of 10^5 K s−1 and shock duration of ~55 ms. Test conditions: Ammonia decomposition in a plug flow reactor at 250–600 °C using 5 vol% NH3 (and 100 vol% NH3 for specific tests) at a gas hourly space velocity (GHSV) of 36 L gcat−1 h−1. Findings: HEA-Co25Mo45 achieved a mass-specific reaction rate of 22.1 gNH3 gmetals−1 h−1 at 500 °C, representing an improvement factor of ~19 versus bimetallic Co-Mo and ~3 versus Ru.; The most active catalyst, HEA-Co25Mo45, reached 50% NH3 conversion (T50) at 422 °C, compared to 600 °C for Ru and 600 °C for bimetallic Co-Mo.; The apparent activation energy (Eapp) varied from 64.7 kJ mol−1 for the most active HEA-Co25Mo45 to 123.1 kJ mol−1 for the least active HEA-Co55Mo15.; Nitrogen desorption energy (ΔEN) for HEA-Co25Mo45 was ~79 kJ mol−1, which is very close to the value for Ru (84 kJ mol−1).; Catalytic activity exhibited a volcano-type behavior with respect to nitrogen adsorption energy, peaking at an optimal ΔEN of ~79 kJ mol−1.; The HEA-Co25Mo45 catalyst showed negligible degradation after ~50 hours of continuous operation at 500 °C.; For pure NH3 decomposition, HEA-Co55Mo15 achieved an improvement factor of ~118 versus bimetallic Co-Mo and ~40 versus Ru.; Atomistic modeling confirmed a single solid-solution phase with δ = 5.4% and ΔHmix = 0.65 kJ mol−1, showing no phase segregation up to 1000 K.. Mechanism: The high catalytic activity is attributed to the robust tuning of surface nitrogen binding strength via the Co/Mo ratio; the optimal activity arises from a tradeoff where Co-rich catalysts bind N too weakly (limiting dehydrogenation) and Mo-rich catalysts bind N too strongly (limiting N2 desorption), with the HEA composition allowing access to the optimal intermediate binding energy (~79 kJ mol−1) predicted by the Sabatier principle.. Limitations: The text notes that the peak intensities in XRD patterns are low due to the much smaller particle sizes compared to previously reported HEAs, and that the bimetallic Co-Mo catalysts are constrained by large miscibility gaps in their phase diagram.. Future work: The authors propose designing practical reactors with cascaded catalyst layers having gradually changing nitrogen binding strengths to match the varying concentration of NH3 along the flow, which can be readily achieved by varying the Co/Mo ratios in HEA catalysts.. Quote: "Quinary CoMoFeNiCu nanoparticles are synthesized in a single solid-solution phase with robust control over the Co/Mo atomic ratio, including those ratios considered to be immiscible according to the Co-Mo bimetallic phase diagram."

card: Paper card. Question: How can high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanocatalysts be synthesized to achieve simultaneous high performance for both hydrogen evolution (HER) and methanol oxidation (MOR) reactions, and what is the mechanism behind their enhanced activity and stability?. System: Pt18Ni26Fe15Co14Cu27 high-entropy alloy nanoparticles supported on carbon (Pt18Ni26Fe15Co14Cu27/C). Processing: One-pot oil phase synthesis at 220 °C for 2 hours at atmospheric pressure using metal acetylacetonate precursors, oleylamine, CTAC, glucose, and Mo(CO)6, followed by acetic acid treatment to remove surfactants and dispersion on Ketjen Black-300 carbon.. Test conditions: HER tested in N2-saturated 1 M KOH (LSV scan rate 5 mV s−1, stability via chronoamperometry at 11 mV and 10,000 CV cycles); MOR tested in N2-saturated 1 M KOH + 1 M CH3OH (CV scan rate 20 mV s−1, stability via chronoamperometry at 0.65 V and 1,000 CV cycles).. Findings: The Pt18Ni26Fe15Co14Cu27/C catalyst exhibits an ultrasmall overpotential of 11 mV at a current density of 10 mA cm−2 for HER, compared to 84 mV for commercial Pt/C.; The mass activity for HER is 10.96 A mg−1Pt at −0.07 V vs. RHE, significantly higher than the 0.83 A mg−1Pt of commercial Pt/C.; The catalyst achieves a mass activity of 15.04 A mg−1Pt for MOR, which is 10 times higher than that of Pt/C (1.45 A mg−1Pt).; The catalyst maintains 99% of its current density after 10 hours of chronoamperometry at 11 mV, whereas Pt/C retains only ~53%.; After 10,000 CV cycles, the Pt18Ni26Fe15Co14Cu27/C catalyst shows no obvious negative shift in overpotential, while Pt/C shifts by ~33 mV.; The Tafel slope for HER is 30 mV dec−1 for the HEA catalyst compared to 98 mV dec−1 for Pt/C, indicating faster kinetics.; CO stripping onset potential is 0.391 V vs. RHE for the HEA catalyst, a 181 mV decrease compared to Pt/C (0.572 V), indicating superior CO anti-poisoning.; DFT calculations reveal a low activation barrier of 0.11 eV for water dissociation and a rate-determining step energy barrier of 0.45 eV for MOR.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the performance to a synergistic effect of multi-active sites on the HEA surface, where different elements (Pt, Ni, Fe, Co, Cu) facilitate specific steps: Pt acts as an electron reservoir, Ni and Co dominate the electroactive region near the Fermi level for electron depletion, and Fe stabilizes intermediates. This configuration enables fast site-to-site electron transfer, efficient water dissociation, and optimal binding strength for intermediates, while the lattice distortion and multi-component nature inhibit CO poisoning and structural degradation.. Limitations: The text notes that slight stoichiometry variations (e.g., changing Cu content) lead to slightly lower activity, though the optimal composition is robust; it also mentions that non-noble metals (Ni, Fe, Co, Cu) may leach slightly during electrocatalysis, causing minor stoichiometry variations, although the overall structure remains stable.. Future work: The authors propose that the simple oil phase synthesis strategy and the understanding of the multi-active sites and fast site-to-site electron transfer mechanism will lay the foundation for the preparation of other HEAs and their application in related electrocatalysis.. Quote: "The Pt18Ni26Fe15Co14Cu27/C catalyst exhibits excellent electrocatalytic performance for hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and methanol oxidation reaction (MOR)."

card: Paper card. Question: How can intrinsically stable single-atom Pd catalysts be fabricated on high-entropy supports to overcome sintering challenges under high-temperature conditions?. System: High-entropy fluorite oxides (CeZrHfTiLa)Ox (HEFO) and Pd1@HEFO (0.5–2.0 wt% Pd loading). Processing: Mechanical milling of metal salt precursors (Ce, Zr, Hf, Ti, La, Pd) with fumed silica followed by pyrolysis at 900 °C in air for 4 h, and subsequent etching of silica with 2.5 M NaOH for 8 h at room temperature. Test conditions: CO oxidation activity measured via light-off curves; hydrothermal stability tested at 750 °C for 10 h in 10 vol% H2O/N2; thermal stability tested at 900 °C; DOC activity at GHSV of 200,000 mL gcat−1 h−1. Findings: Pd1@HEFO exhibits an onset temperature for CO oxidation of ~80 °C, compared to 223 °C for Pd@CeO2.; Complete CO oxidation for Pd1@HEFO occurs at 170 °C, whereas Pd@CeO2 requires 253 °C.; The apparent activation energy (Ea) for Pd1@HEFO is 43.40 kJ/mol, significantly lower than 72.21 kJ/mol for Pd@CeO2.; CO chemisorption determined 6.44% surface Pd atoms (0.0644 μmol CO/μmol Pd), confirming isolated Pd sites.; The ratio of surface chemisorbed oxygen (Oβ) to lattice oxygen (Oα) in Pd1@HEFO is about twofold higher than in Pd@CeO2.; Pd1@HEFO retains structural integrity and single-atom dispersion after hydrothermal treatment at 750 °C for 10 h.; Post-deposition Pd/HEFO-p sintered and aggregated after treatment at 900 °C, unlike the mechanochemically synthesized Pd1@HEFO.. Mechanism: The formation of (PdyCeZrHfTiLa)Ox solid solution is an entropy-dominated process where high configurational entropy decreases Gibbs free energy, stabilizing isolated Pd atoms within the HEFO sublattice via Pd–O–M bonds. This structure enhances the reducibility of surface lattice oxygen and creates oxygen vacancies, facilitating the Mars–van Krevelen mechanism for CO oxidation.. Limitations: Pd atoms in Pd1@HEFO are not stable in reductive atmospheres (e.g., H2 treatment), making the catalyst more suitable for oxygen-rich conditions like diesel exhaust oxidation.. Future work: The authors suggest this entropy-driven methodology may guide the development of next-generation single-atom catalysts.. Quote: "Here, we report a novel entropy-driven strategy to stabilize Pd single-atom on the high-entropy fluorite oxides (CeZrHfTiLa)Ox (HEFO) as the support by a combination of mechanical milling with calcination at 900 °C."

card: Paper card. Question: How can multi-elemental alloy nanoparticles (MEA-NPs) composed of traditionally immiscible elements be rationally designed and rapidly synthesized to achieve high catalytic efficiency and durability for ammonia decomposition?. System: RuRhCoNi (Ru-4 MEA-NPs) and RuRhCoNiIr (Ru-5 MEA-NPs) nanoparticles; precursor elements: Ru, Rh, Co, Ni, Ir, Pd, Cr, Fe, Cu, Mo. Processing: Rapid high-temperature synthesis via electrical Joule heating: multi-elemental salt precursors (0.05 M in ethanol) deposited on activated carbon nanofibers, heated to 1500 K for 500 ms (0.5 s), followed by quenching. Test conditions: Catalytic NH3 decomposition in a fixed-bed flow reactor at atmospheric pressure; gas hourly space velocity (GHSV) ≥30,000; reaction temperatures stepped from 300°C to 550°C; in situ stability testing in electron microscope up to 873 K for 30 min per point. Findings: Ru-4 MEA-NPs reached 100% NH3 decomposition at ~470°C, whereas a pure Ru sample with similar loading showed only 30% conversion.; MEA-NPs exhibited an ultrasmall and uniform particle size distribution of ~3 to 5 nm.; Ru atoms in Ru-5 MEA-NPs diffuse approximately 100 times slower than in a binary Ru-Ni alloy, indicating sluggish diffusion.; The Ru-5 MEA-NPs maintained a homogeneous alloy structure and uniform dispersion after in situ annealing up to 873 K.; Ru-5 MEA-NPs outperformed a Ru-5 sample prepared by impregnation (annealed at 300°C for 1 hour), confirming the alloy structure's role in performance.; The alloy formation temperature for Ru-Ni bimetallic is ~2000 K, while it decreases to 871 K for Ru-4 and 584 K for Ru-5 MEA-NPs due to entropy effects.; MEA-NPs showed a fragmented domain structure with rich interfaces, unlike the single domain structure of pure Ru NPs.. Mechanism: Entropy-driven thermodynamic stabilization (increased mixing entropy lowers Gibbs free energy) combined with kinetic stabilization (sluggish diffusion caused by lattice distortion and atomic size mismatch) prevents phase separation and elemental segregation, enabling the formation of uniform alloy structures from immiscible elements.. Limitations: DFT calculations did not account for vibrational energy and surface-energy effects in nanoparticles, meaning predicted formation temperatures represent a thermodynamic lower limit; short-range chemical ordering exists, meaning the alloy is not completely random.. Future work: The computationally aided rational design and rapid synthesis method can be generally used to accelerate catalyst discovery in multi-elemental materials for various catalytic reactions.. Quote: "We report the computationally aided, entropy-driven design and synthesis of highly efficient and durable catalyst MEA-NPs."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the electronic structure of platinum group metal-based high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles influence their hydrogen evolution reaction activity and stability compared to conventional catalysts?. System: IrPdPtRhRu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles (approx. 20 at% each of Ru, Rh, Pd, Ir, Pt). Processing: One-pot polyol process: five metal precursors in equimolar ratio dissolved in H2O, added to preheated triethylene glycol containing PVP (K30, MW ≈ 40,000) at 230 °C, cooled to RT, washed with ethanol/water/ether, and vacuum dried at RT. Test conditions: HER activity measured in 0.05 M H2SO4 and 1.0 M KOH electrolytes; scan rate 5 mV s−1; rotation speed 1600 rpm; stability tested via 3000 cyclic voltammetry cycles at 100 mV s−1. Findings: HEA NPs have a mean diameter of 5.5 ± 1.2 nm and an fcc structure with a lattice parameter of a = 3.856(1) Å.; The valence band spectrum of HEA NPs is broad and featureless without obvious peaks, unlike monometallic NPs which show obvious peaks.; At an overpotential of 25 mV, the turnover frequency (TOF) of HEA NPs was 9.5 times higher than commercial Pt/C in 0.05 M H2SO4.; At an overpotential of 25 mV, the TOF of HEA NPs was 7.8 times higher than commercial Pt/C in 1.0 M KOH.; HEA NPs required overpotentials of 33.0 mV (acidic) and 17.0 mV (alkaline) to achieve 10 mA cmgeo−2, significantly lower than monometallic counterparts.; HEA NPs showed no apparent loss in current density after 3000 cycles, whereas commercial Pt/C lost 35.5 mV in overpotential at 10 mA cmgeo−2.; The high HER activity of HEA NPs does not follow the conventional d-band center theory trend observed for monometallic catalysts.. Mechanism: The broad and featureless valence band spectrum implies random atomic configurations leading to a variety of local electronic structures and diverse local density of states, which allows for superior HER activity that cannot be simply estimated from the d-band center theory.. Limitations: The interpretation of properties is challenging; the d-band center theory cannot describe the activity of HEAs due to surface heterogeneity; the authors note deviations in d-band center calculations may originate from differences between NPs and simple slab models.. Future work: It would be useful to use a combination of density functional theory calculations and machine learning to understand the reaction mechanism; HEA NPs can be a major future research target given the uncountable combinations.. Quote: "The observed valence band (VB) spectrum are broad without any peaks which implies that the HEA NPs have random atomic configurations leading to a variety of local electronic structures."

card: Paper card. Question: What thermodynamic factors and specific elemental additions dictate the occurrence of liquid phase separation (LPS) versus single-phase solidification in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), and how do these factors influence microstructure formation?. System: High-entropy alloys (HEAs), multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs), and complex concentrated alloys (CCAs), specifically systems containing Co, Cr, Cu, Fe, Ni, Mn, Al, Ti, V, Nb, Ag, Sn, Mo, and Y2O3 (e.g., CoCrCuFeNi, AgAlCoCrCuNi, CoCrCu, CoCrCuNi, CoCrCuFeNi, CoCrCuMnNi, CoCrCuNiV, AlCoCrCuFeNiSi0.5). Processing: Arc-melting, induction melting, laser cladding, electromagnetic levitation, rapid solidification, and undercooling experiments (e.g., drop tube, molten fused silica fluxing); specific undercooling temperatures noted include ~150 K, 160 K, 190 K, 293 K, and 381 K (0.23Tm). Test conditions: Solidification from liquid state under varying cooling rates (slow cooling, rapid solidification), undercooling past critical temperatures (ΔTcrit), and in-situ neutron transmission imaging during heating and cooling of CoCrCu alloys. Findings: Positive mixing enthalpy (ΔHmix) not compensated by entropy of mixing leads to liquid phase separation.; Co, Ni, and Ti promote miscibility in HEAs/CCAs/MPEAs, while Cr, V, and Nb raise the miscibility gap temperature and increase LPS.; Addition of appropriate amounts of Ni to equiatomic CoCrCu eliminates immiscibility, allowing CoCrCuNi, CoCrCuFeNi, and CoCrCuMnNi to solidify dendritically.; Only three out of ten tested additions to equiatomic CoCrCu (Ni, Fe, Mn) resulted in dendritic solidification; the rest underwent stable LPS.; In CoCrCuFeNi, metastable LPS occurs when undercooling exceeds ΔTcrit values of 100 K (Guo et al.), 160 K (x=1.0), 190 K (x=1.5), and 293 K (x=2.0).; In AgAlCoCrCuNi, the addition of Ag caused phase separation into Cu-rich globules embedded in Cu-depleted phases.; The addition of 1 wt.% nanosized Y2O3 to AlCoCrCuFeNiSi0.5 caused liquids to separate into egg-like globules of Cu-rich liquids inside Cu-depleted liquid.; LPS in CoCrCuFeNi significantly decreases yield strength and elongation due to microstructure non-uniformity.. Mechanism: Liquid phase separation is driven by positive deviations from Raoult's law and positive enthalpy of mixing (ΔHmix > 0), which creates a preference for nearest neighbors of similar atoms. When the enthalpy term (ΔHmix) exceeds the entropy term (TΔS) in the Gibbs free energy equation, the system decomposes into two immiscible liquids (L1 + L2). In metastable cases, undercooling allows the alloy to enter a miscibility gap beneath the liquidus curve that is not present in equilibrium conditions. Constitutional LPS occurs when compositional changes in the interdendritic liquid during solidification trigger separation.. Limitations: The text notes that it is impossible to visualize the phase diagram space of multicomponent alloy systems containing 5+ elements, making it difficult to predict liquid phase separation without computational screening. Additionally, the lack of experimental data for mixing enthalpies of many binary alloys necessitates the use of models like Miedema's for approximations.. Future work: The authors suggest the need for creative ideas to understand the nature of solidification in multicomponent alloys due to the impossibility of orthogonal element phase diagram visualization. They also highlight the need to amend ΔHmix criteria for predicting single-phase formation to include the possibility of liquid phase separation when ΔHmix > 0.. Quote: "Positive mixing enthalpy if not compensated by the entropy of mixing will lead to liquid phase separation."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the addition of Ni to the immiscible equiatomic CoCrCu system affect liquid state miscibility and solidification behavior, and can in-situ neutron imaging capture this remixing process?. System: Equiatomic CoCrCu buttons with added elemental Ni buttons to form equiatomic CoCrCuNi (CoCrCu + Ni). Processing: Arc-melted CoCrCu buttons and remelted Ni buttons placed in an alumina crucible inside a high-temperature vacuum furnace (HOT-A furnace) at ≈1 × 10−6 mbar; heated to 1500 °C, held for 150 radiographs (approx. 35 min), then cooled to 1000 °C. Test conditions: In-situ neutron imaging at CG-1D Neutron Imaging Instrument using cold neutrons (0.8 < λ < 6 Å); 10 radiographs acquired every 20 °C from 1000 °C to 1500 °C and back to 1000 °C; ramp rate 20 °C/min; acquisition time 10 s/radiograph; spatial resolution ~200 μm. Findings: Onset of melting observed at approximately 1100 °C, with complete dissolution of phases at ~1420 °C.; Solidification of the CoCrCuNi alloy initiates at ~1320 °C.; No changes in neutron attenuation were observed during the solidification of the CoCrCuNi alloy, indicating solidification from a single-phase liquid.; Thermodynamic calculations indicate the CoCrCuNix alloy solidifies from a single-phase liquid when x ≥ 0.275, close to the nominal concentration of x = 0.25.; The CT images of the solidified CoCrCuNi alloy show uniform contrast with no macroscopic-phase separations, unlike the heterogeneous CoCrCu alloy.; The miscibility gap in the CoCrCu system is eliminated by the addition of Ni, allowing the Cu-rich liquid to enter the solution.; The furnace thermocouple temperature is estimated to be about 15 °C higher than the sample during heating.. Mechanism: Ni acts as a solubility pathway for the Cu-rich liquid phase to enter the solution with the overall melt, transforming the previously immiscible CoCr-rich and Cu-rich liquids into a single-phase liquid upon dissolution.. Limitations: The accuracy of the temperature measurements is within ±15 °C due to the difference between furnace thermocouple readings and actual sample temperature.. Future work: The authors propose that in-situ neutron imaging of solidification can provide a novel solution to probe the liquid phases of calculated isopleths and provide valuable insight into the liquid state behavior of HEAs.. Quote: "The neutron imaging shows that the solidification of CoCrCuNi results from a single-phase liquid."

card: Paper card. Question: How does increasing the configurational entropy by introducing multiple salts into a liquid electrolyte impact the thermodynamic and kinetic properties, specifically solvation structures, ion transport, and interphase stability, in lithium batteries?. System: 0.6 M High-Entropy (HE) electrolyte composed of 0.15 M LiFSI, 0.15 M LiTFSI, 0.15 M LiDFOB, and 0.15 M LiNO3 in dimethoxyethane (DME) solvent; compared against single-salt electrolytes (0.6 M LiFSI-DME, 0.6 M LiTFSI-DME, 0.6 M LiDFOB-DME) and a 0.36 M LiNO3-DME electrolyte.. Processing: Electrolytes prepared by dissolving specific amounts of lithium salts (LiFSI, LiTFSI, LiDFOB, LiNO3) in DME solvent in an Ar-filled glove box (H2O < 0.1 ppm, O2 < 0.1 ppm) at room temperature; total lithium ion concentration maintained at 0.6 M for the HE electrolyte.. Test conditions: Electrochemical cycling in CR2032 coin cells at room temperature; Li||LiFePO4 cells (2.5–5.0 V) for oxidation stability; Li||NCM811 cells (2.8–4.3 V) for cathode compatibility; Li||Cu cells for plating/stripping efficiency; Li||Li4Ti5O12 cells for rate capability; symmetric Li||Li cells for impedance and transference number; Cryo-TEM at -170 °C; Operando 7Li NMR; Raman spectroscopy at room temperature.. Findings: The 0.6 M HE-DME electrolyte exhibits a 7Li NMR chemical shift of -0.68 ppm, indicating weaker solvation interaction compared to single-salt electrolytes (e.g., -1.19 ppm for LiTFSI-DME).; The 0.6 M HE-DME electrolyte shows an oxidation stability limit up to ~4.51 V, higher than the 4.36 V limit of the 0.6 M LiFSI-DME control.; Lithium plating/stripping in the 0.6 M HE-DME electrolyte achieves a Coulombic efficiency of up to 98.6%, considerably higher than the 0.6 M LiFSI-DME electrolyte.; The 0.6 M HE-DME electrolyte has a lithium-ion transference number of 0.46 and ionic conductivity of ~12.1 mS cm−1, compared to 0.39 and 9.6 mS cm−1 for the LiFSI-DME electrolyte.; At a rate of 5.0 C, the 0.6 M HE-DME electrolyte retains ~115 mAh g−1 capacity in Li||Li4Ti5O12 cells, whereas the LiFSI-DME electrolyte retains only ~40 mAh g−1.; Li||NCM811 cells with 0.6 M HE-DME electrolyte achieve over 82% capacity retention after 100 cycles at 0.333 C charged to 4.3 V.; Long-term cycling at 6.0 C in Li||NCM811 cells shows ~85% capacity retention after 500 cycles and ~80% after 600 cycles.; Cryo-TEM reveals a thin (~6 nm) inorganic-rich SEI in the HE-DME electrolyte, contrasting with a thicker, non-uniform, solvent-decomposition-dominated SEI in the LiFSI-DME electrolyte.. Mechanism: The introduction of multiple salts creates a diversity of anionic groups that participate in solvation structures, resulting in a larger variety of lithium-ion solvation environments (over 30 types predicted by DFT). This entropy-dominated diversity weakens the solvation strength between lithium ions and solvents/anions, facilitating lithium-ion diffusivity and charge transfer. The weaker solvation and diverse anion participation lead to the formation of inorganic-rich, stable interphase layers (SEI/CEI) that suppress solvent decomposition and dendrite growth.. Limitations: The text notes that the DME solvent has relatively low oxidation stability, which is a challenge for high-voltage cathodes, although the HE electrolyte mitigates this. The study focuses on a specific four-salt prototype, and the compositional landscape is described as huge and largely unexplored.. Future work: The authors propose that the compositional landscape of HE materials is huge and suggest that raising entropy by introducing multiple salts can be used to improve functional properties, where the choice of specific salts and solvents should be guided by their interactions with specific anode and cathode chemistry. They also mention preparing a five-component salt HE electrolyte to support even longer stable cycling.. Quote: "Unlike all liquid electrolytes so far reported, the participation of several anionic groups in this electrolyte induces a larger diversity in solvation structures, unexpectedly decreasing solvation strengths between lithium ions and solvents/anions."

Paper card. Question: How do single and high-entropy (HE) electrolyte systems with different lithium salts and concentrations behave at the molecular level?. System: High entropy liquid electrolytes with different lithium salts in dimethoxyethane (DME) solvent; specific ratio of 1:10 salt/solvent. Processing: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations using LAMMPS with OPLS-AA force field; system packing via Packmol (60 × 60 × 60 Å box, 1200 DME + 120 salt molecules); energy minimization via conjugate-gradient; isothermal-isobaric ensemble at 300 K for 5 ns; canonical ensemble equilibration for 6 ns followed by 10 ns production run with 0.5 fs time-step; DFT calculations using Gaussian 09 with B3LYP/6-31 + G(d,p) for geometry and B3LYP/6-311 + +G(3df,3dp) for energy. Test conditions: 300 K (room temperature); cut-off distance of 1.1 nm for Lennard-Jones interactions; snapshots obtained every 0.5 ps. Findings: Simulation boxes were randomly packed with 1200 molecules of DME and 120 salt molecules to achieve a 1:10 salt/solvent ratio; Isothermal-isobaric ensemble simulations at 300 K were performed for 5 ns to obtain correct volumes; Canonical ensemble simulations were continued for another 10 ns after equilibration; Radial density functions and diffusivities of lithium ions were computed using the MDAnalysis package; Solvation structures were analyzed using the Python Materials Genomics (pymatgen) package; Partial charges were computed using Møller–Plesset second-order perturbation method with cc-pVTZ(-f) basis set. Quote: "Molecules and ions were described by the optimized potentials for a liquid simulations all-atom (OPLS-AA) force field."

card: Paper card. Question: How do additive manufacturing processing parameters and feedstock material types (pre-alloyed vs. mixed elemental) influence the microstructure, phase composition, density, and mechanical properties of high entropy alloys?. System: CrMnFeCoNi, AlCrFeCoNi, Al0.3CrFeCoNi, FeCoCrNi, NbMoTaW, VNbMoTaW, AlXCrFeCoNi, AlXCrFeNi2Cu, TiZrHfNb, FeCoNiCr, and composites with TiC or W reinforcement. Processing: Powder Bed Fusion (L-PBF, EB-PBF), Direct Energy Deposition (BPD, WAAM, WLAM), Binder Jetting, and Material Extrusion; parameters include laser energy density, scan velocity, layer thickness, hatch spacing, pre-heating (up to 1100 °C), and post-processing sintering or annealing (e.g., 900 °C, 1100 °C). Test conditions: As-built conditions and post-heat treatment conditions; high-temperature oxidation testing; corrosion testing in harsh environments; tensile testing for yield strength and ultimate tensile strength. Findings: L-PBF produces the highest yield strength and UTS in CrMnFeCoNi due to high cooling rates, but results in reduced elongation compared to DED.; Annealing at 900 °C decomposes dislocation networks in FeCoCrNi, reducing residual stress, while 1100 °C further reduces stress and forms twin-rich grains.; Using mixed elemental powder in PBF requires higher laser energy density than pre-alloyed powder to achieve adequate synthesis and density.; EB-PBF pre-heating (up to 1100 °C) causes element segregation in AlCrFeCoNi, leading to a higher fraction of FCC phase at the bottom of the part compared to the top.; Adding Al (X=0.75) to AlXCrFeNi2Cu HEA via L-PBF forms a cellular FCC dendrite with a B2 matrix, reducing crack propagation compared to the columnar FCC structure of the base alloy.; CrFeCoNi pre-alloyed powder mixed with Cu and Ti powders showed optimal energy density varying due to melting point differences (CrFeCoNi: 1414 °C, Cu: 1084 °C, Ti: 1688 °C).; Sintering AlCrFeCoNi at 900 °C in Binder Jetting forms an undesired sigma phase, while sintering above 1200 °C results in a single BCC phase.; Higher energy density in L-PBF reduces defects like pores, enhancing corrosion resistance in AlCrFeCoNi, whereas EB-PBF pre-heating can create Cr-depleted pitting sites.. Mechanism: The authors argue that rapid solidification in L-PBF prevents element segregation but creates high residual stress and dislocation networks, while the thermal cycles in DED and pre-heating in EB-PBF act as in-situ heat treatments causing segregation and phase transformations (e.g., BCC to FCC). The synthesis of HEAs from mixed elemental powders is hindered by different melting points and segregation tendencies, requiring higher energy density for in-situ alloying. Post-processing heat treatments modify microstructures by relieving stress, recrystallizing grains, or inducing secondary phase formation depending on temperature and atmosphere.. Limitations: The text states that synthesizing HEAs using mixed elemental powder remains challenging due to elemental segregation and different melting points. Imperfections such as volume defects and elemental segregation can serve as corrosion initiation sites. EB-PBF pre-heating causes microstructural changes between the bottom and top sections. The fabrication of pre-alloyed wires is significantly more expensive and complex. Inadequate parameters can lead to over-melting, vaporization, or incomplete fusion.. Future work: The authors emphasize the need for further research on lightweight HEAs and regular updates on the latest developments. They propose that future success should focus on adequate synthesis and physical properties, specifically regarding microstructural defects, and recommend using mixed elemental substances or combined cable wires to reduce costs while ensuring proper selection of grain size, morphology, and wire diameters.. Quote: "synthesizing HEAs such as CrFeCoNi and CrMnFeCoNi HEAs by AM using mixed elemental powder remains challenging due to issues such as elemental segregation and the different melting points of the elements"

card: Paper card. Question: How do additive manufacturing (AM) techniques and post-heat treatments influence the microstructure, mechanical properties, and deformation mechanisms of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) compared to conventional casting methods?. System: CoCrFeNi, AlxCoCrFeNi (x=0.3, 0.6, 0.85), CoCrFeMnNi, FeCoCrAlCu, Ti25Zr50Nb0Ta25, CoCrFeNiTi, and AA5083/CoCrFeNi composites. Processing: Selective Laser Melting (SLM), Laser Metal Deposition (LMD/DMD/DLF), and Selective Electron Beam Melting (SEBM); parameters include layer thickness (20–100 μm), volumetric energy density (VED), laser power (e.g., 400 W), scanning speed (e.g., 1200 mm/s), and pre-heating; post-treatments include High Isostatic Pressing (HIP) at 1100 °C for 2 h, annealing (750–1000 °C), and solution treatment.. Test conditions: Tensile and compression tests at room temperature (298 K) and cryogenic temperature (77 K); microstructural analysis via XRD, SEM, TEM, and EBSD; wear resistance testing.. Findings: AM-processed HEAs exhibit superior yield strength and ductility compared to casting counterparts due to fine microstructures formed by rapid solidification.; SLM CoCrFeNi specimens showed significantly higher yield strength than arc-melt specimens while retaining significant ductility.; Increasing volumetric energy density (VED) in SLM CoCrFeMnNi reduced holes and cracks, leading to higher ultimate tensile strength.; HIP treatment at 1100 °C for 2 h removed second-phase grain-boundary phases and segregation in Al0.3CoCrFeNi, achieving chemical homogenization.; SEBM AlCoCrFeNi specimens displayed better plasticity than cast specimens due to finer grains and a substantial fraction of ductile FCC phase.; Cryogenic testing (77 K) on LAM-fabricated CrMnFeCoNi HEA enhanced yield strength and ductility, with deformation twinning becoming more obvious at high strain.; Solution treatment of SEBM CoCrFeNiTi HEA improved ductility without lowering strength by removing needle-like Ni3Ti precipitates.; Different AM methods induce substantial differences in yield strength and plasticity; for instance, DLF Al0.3CoCrFeNi showed much lower yield strength compared to SLM and SEBM methods.. Mechanism: The enhanced mechanical properties are primarily ascribed to the refinement of microstructures caused by large temperature gradients and rapid solidification during AM, which leads to fine cellular dendrite structures, high dislocation densities, and suppressed elemental segregation. Post-treatments like HIP and annealing further enhance properties by removing fabrication defects (pores, microcracks) and releasing residual stress, while specific heat treatments can dissolve or modify precipitates (e.g., Ni3Ti, B2 phases) to optimize the balance between strength and ductility.. Limitations: Defects such as residual stress, microcracks, and pores exist in as-built AM components, degrading mechanical properties; some AM specimens exhibit anisotropy in mechanical properties due to texture and grain orientation; limited ductility is observed in some Al-rich alloys due to brittle phase appearance; most existing studies focus on tension/compression, with rare data on fracture toughness, fatigue, oxidation, irradiation, or corrosion.. Future work: Optimize processing parameters and heat treatment regimes to improve microstructures and reduce residual stress; investigate fracture toughness, fatigue, oxidation, irradiation, and corrosion properties; expand research to light-weight and refractory HEAs; develop broader compositional ranges; investigate materials with large differences in melting temperatures; and study effective powder blending methods to reduce agglomeration and increase homogeneity.. Quote: "Compared with the casting counterparts, AM-HEAs were found to have a superior yield strength and ductility as a consequence of the fine microstructure formed during the rapid solidification in the fabrication process."

card: Paper card. Question: Can a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy be successfully fabricated via selective laser melting (SLM) despite the high melting points of its constituent elements, and what are the resulting microstructural, mechanical, and corrosion properties compared to traditional superalloys?. System: NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (nominal equiatomic composition: Nb 99.9%, Mo 99.9%, Ta 99.9%, W 99.9%). Processing: Selective Laser Melting (SLM) using FORWEDO LM120 equipment with a 500 W fiber laser in an argon atmosphere (<20 ppm oxygen); initial parameters: hatch distance 0.1 mm, layer thickness 0.1 mm, laser power factor 0.8, scanning velocity 250 mm/s, S-cross scanning; followed by a remelting process (3 total passes per layer) to achieve a linear energy density of up to 2.83 J/mm. Test conditions: Microstructure and composition analyzed via SEM (HITACHI SU-8010) and EDS; crystal structure via XRD (Cu target, λ = 1.54 Å); microhardness measured on XY plane; corrosion resistance tested via potentiodynamic polarization in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution (scanning voltage −0.2 V to +0.2 V) and high-voltage scanning (−1.5 to +2 V). Findings: A single BCC solid solution was formed without secondary phases, with an experimental lattice parameter of 3.2034 Å.; Elements with lower melting points and densities (Nb and Mo) showed negative molar ratio deviations of up to 3.5% (Nb: −3.5 at%, Mo: −0.16 at%) compared to the nominal 25%.; The average grain size was 13.4 μm, significantly smaller than the 200 μm observed in as-cast NbMoTaW HEA.; Primary and secondary dendrite arm spacings were 6.59 μm and 1.68 μm, respectively, much finer than the 20–30 μm spacing in as-cast samples.; The average microhardness of the SLM-fabricated sample reached 826 Hv, compared to 446 Hv for arc-melted HEA and 310–437 Hv for superalloys.; The free-corrosion current (Icorr) of the NbMoTaW HEA was 8.716 × 10−11 A, which is two orders of magnitude lower than that of 316 L steel (8.815 × 10−9 A).; Visual corrosion testing showed 316 L steel suffered up to 1 mm corrosion depth, while the NbMoTaW alloy exhibited only crack extension and minor pitting.. Mechanism: The rapid solidification in SLM creates extremely high temperature gradients and cooling rates, limiting growth time and resulting in fine grains and slender dendrites. Composition deviations occur because powders with lower melting points and densities fuse first, spread over larger areas, absorb more energy, and evaporate earlier during the process. The improved hardness is attributed to grain refinement following the Hall–Petch law, while superior corrosion resistance is due to the presence of easily passivating elements (Nb, Mo, Ta) despite minor segregation.. Limitations: The ductility of the NbMoTaW HEA at room temperature remains low, and while composition deviation exists (up to 3.5%), it is noted that further study of mechanical properties is still necessary.. Future work: Further study of mechanical properties is required to fully assess the potential of the SLM-fabricated NbMoTaW HEA.. Quote: "The HEA shows an excellent microstructure, microhardness, and corrosion resistance performance compared with traditional superalloys."

card: Paper card. Question: How does increasing compositional complexity and specific alloying elements in additively manufactured refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) affect helium bubble size, density, and distribution under high-energy helium irradiation compared to pure tungsten?. System: NbTa, MoNbTa, MoNbTaW, NbTaVW (additively manufactured RHEAs) and pure W (commercial rolled sheet). Processing: Laser beam directed energy deposition (LB-DED) using elemental Mo, Nb, Ta, V, and W powders; laser powers ranged from 400–750 W (NbTa), 220–350 W (MoNbTa), 1800 W (MoNbTaW), and 800–1000 W (NbTaVW); laser scan velocities 300–600 mm/min; layer thickness 250 µm; substrates preheated to 200–300 °C for NbTa and NbTaVW; pure W was a 2 mm thick rolled sheet cut into 5 mm discs. Test conditions: 200 keV He+ ion bombardment at 900 °C to a fluence of 1 × 10^17 cm^-2 at a flux of ~3 × 10^13 cm^-2 s^-1. Findings: As compositional complexity increased from MoNb to MoNbTa to MoNbTaW, the average He bubble size decreased while the areal density increased.; The NbTaVW RHEA exhibited the largest He bubble diameters (13 nm) compared to the MoNbTaW RHEA (1 nm) due to V segregation.; The pure W control sample had the smallest average bubble diameter (5 nm) and smallest grain size (275 nm), with bubbles accumulating at grain boundaries.; In the NbTaVW sample, V segregation occurred in intercellular/interdendritic regions, and He bubbles accumulated specifically at these V-rich regions.; The average grain size of the NbTaVW sample was ~24 µm, approximately 100 times larger than the W control sample.; No irradiation-induced surface nanofeatures were observed on the SEM scale for any sample following He implantation.; The areal number density of bubbles showed an inverse relationship to size: as bubbles grew larger, their density decreased.. Mechanism: Increasing compositional complexity and entropy generally limits He bubble size, likely due to lattice distortion effects and changes in melting temperature and elastic modulus. However, the addition of V leads to segregation during AM processing; V has the lowest melting point and lowest binding energy of He to a vacancy, allowing rapid He accumulation into larger bubbles. The net flux of vacancies towards bubbles and larger atoms (Nb, Ta, W) away from bubbles results in V enrichment at the bubbles. Grain boundaries in pure W act as sinks, limiting intragranular bubble size, whereas the large grains in AM RHEAs allow for larger bubbles unless compositional complexity is optimized.. Limitations: The study notes that the RHEAs have much larger grain sizes (10s of µm) compared to the commercial W (300 nm), which significantly influences bubble density and size; the lack of post-fabrication grain refinement in the AM alloys may mask their full potential. Additionally, the study only investigated He irradiation and did not assess fracture properties, recrystallization performance, or high-temperature mechanical behavior.. Future work: Future studies will elucidate the mechanical performance and high-temperature performance of the RHEAs studied here, including the potential for self-healing. Further exploration is needed on how post-fabrication treatments to reduce grain sizes could improve bubble characteristics, and the performance of these alloys in other reactor-relevant areas like fracture properties.. Quote: "As the RHEA complexity increases from MoNb, to MoNbTa, to MoNbTaW, the He bubble size decreases, while the density increases."

card: Paper card. Question: What designing and regulating strategies can optimize the catalytic performance of multicomponent high-entropy materials (HEMs), and what are the underlying mechanisms revealed by theory and experiment?. System: Multicomponent high-entropy alloys (HEAs), oxides (HEOs), layered double hydroxides (LDHs), perovskites, MOFs, sulfides, phosphides, and (oxy)hydroxides; specific examples include PtRuNiCoFeMo nanowires, Pt18Ni26Fe15Co14Cu27 nanoparticles, AlNiCoRuMoFeCrTi HEOs, and PdCuMoNiCo hollow spheres.. Processing: Various methods including arc melting, low-temperature oil phase synthesis, pyrolysis of MOFs, galvanic exchange reactions, dealloying of Al-based or Mn-based precursors, mechanochemical milling, Ar plasma etching, metal-tannin coordination assembly, sol-gel methods, Joule heating for intermetallic formation, and high-temperature carbon shock synthesis.. Test conditions: Electrochemical tests in alkaline media (e.g., 0.5 M H2SO4, alkaline solutions) for reactions including hydrogen oxidation (HOR), hydrogen evolution (HER), methanol oxidation (MOR), glycerol oxidation (GOR), ethanol oxidation (EOR), oxygen reduction (ORR), oxygen evolution (OER), CO oxidation, and CO2 reduction; also tested in Li-O2 batteries and for photocatalytic water splitting.. Findings: PtRuNiCoFeMo HEA nanowires with 1.8 ± 0.3 nm diameter achieved mass activity of 6.75 A mgPt+Ru−1 and specific activity of 8.96 mA cm−2 for HOR, which are 4.1 and 19.8 times higher than commercial PtRu/C and Pt/C, respectively.; NiCoFePtRh ultrasmall sub-2 nm HEA nanoparticles achieved a mass activity of 28.3 A mg−1 for HER, which is 40.4 times larger than commercial Pt/C.; Quinary AlNiCoRuMo nanoporous alloy/oxide system exhibited much better activities for HER, OER, and ORR compared to ternary and quaternary samples, with only 20 at% Ru content.; 8-component AlNiCoRuMoFeCrTi HEO showed OER/ORR activities comparable to the quinary AlNiCoRuMo but with reduced Ru content (12.5% in theory) due to a Cr–Fe synergistic effect.; PdCuMoNiCo hollow spherical nanoparticles exhibited higher specific surface area and bi-functional activity for formic acid oxidation and ORR compared to solid counterparts.; High-entropy perovskite cobaltate with five equimolar metals achieved an overpotential of 320 mV at 10 mA cm−2 for OER, with the high configuration entropy facilitating a shift from the adsorbate evolution mechanism to the lattice oxygen mechanism (LOM).; Pt25Pd25Ni25P25 amorphous HEA exhibited 5- and 10-fold higher HER activity in alkaline solutions compared to ternary Pt60Ni15P25 and Pd40Ni40P20 amorphous alloys, respectively.; Five-component (MoWVNbTa)S2 high-entropy dichalcogenide achieved a high current density of 0.51 A cm−2 and turnover frequency of 58.3 s−1 for CO2 reduction to CO.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the random distribution of different metal elements in HEMs contributes to transcendental homogeneity and unexpected synergistic effects that stimulate the kinetic barrier for adsorption/desorption. The 'cocktail effect' and entropy stabilization allow for tunable electronic structures, where specific elements can adjust the local density of states (LDOS) and d-band centers of active sites. Defects (like oxygen vacancies) and strain effects further modulate adsorption energies, while the high configurational entropy can facilitate the formation of oxygen vacancies and shift reaction mechanisms (e.g., to LOM). In ordered intermetallics, specific site isolation and optimized adsorption configurations reduce energy barriers.. Limitations: The authors state that 'the relationships between the structural effects and catalytic properties of HEMs are still unambiguous', making it difficult to purposely regulate intrinsic surface electronic states. They note that 'we cannot mix any five or more components in one nanostructure without phase separation, especially for these enthalpy-dominated systems'. Additionally, 'the entropy value is usually not related to the catalytic activity', and thorough comparisons of 'best' catalysts are often impossible due to the 'numberless combinations'.. Future work: The authors propose that 'a high throughput fabrication strategy is highly needed to prepare more samples for catalyst screening' and that 'developing a novel strategy such as high throughout DFT calculation and machine learning to determine the element combination for a specific chemical reaction is very urgent'. They also suggest that 'for a specific reaction, the phase or element separation may result in a better activity considering the rich interface and possible stepwise reaction on different sites of the heterostructure'.. Quote: "The random distribution of different metal elements in HEMs could contribute to transcendental homogeneity, leading to an unexpected synergistic effect to stimulate the kinetic barrier for adsorption/desorption."

Paper card. Question: How can the active sites of high-entropy catalysts be identified and how can their performance be enhanced through design strategies?. System: High-entropy oxides (HEOs)/noble metal composites, single-crystal high-entropy metals (HEMs), and multicomponent catalysts with more than 12 or 14 elements. Findings: The real active sites of high-entropy catalysts for many reactions are still misty, especially for more complicated high-entropy systems such as HEOs/noble metal composites.; Single-crystal HEMs are extremely hard to achieve due to the extensive existence of crystalline lattice strains, lattice distortions, and numerous unsaturated defects.; An equal atomic ratio does not always lead to the highest activity although the highest entropy value is achieved.; The surface states may be completely different from the bulk composites and the surface may be severely oxidized if many active elements are incorporated.; The rich and tunable chemical coordination environment in HEMs makes it possible to incorporate a large amount of single atom catalysts.. Mechanism: The authors argue that high-entropy design, by incorporating more elements into one system, allows for exploring synergistic effects between elements to enhance catalytic performance (activity and stability) or reduce noble metal content. They suggest that multicomponent catalysts can enhance reaction selectivity by changing the conventional reaction path, and that the tunable chemical coordination environment in HEMs facilitates atomic interaction studies.. Limitations: The reported so-called best high-entropy (multicomponent) samples may still need further optimization; the surface states may be completely different from the bulk composites and the surface may be severely oxidized; single-crystal HEMs are extremely hard to achieve due to lattice strains and defects; preparing single atom catalysts with ultrahigh loading via a simple method is challenging.. Future work: Developing an advanced synthesis strategy for the preparation of single-crystal HEMs and high-entropy materials with precisely controlled nanostructures; developing high throughput synthesis or DFT calculation strategies to screen the most efficient catalysts; preparing single atom catalysts with ultrahigh loading; in situ monitoring of the surface atomic/electronic structural changes; incorporating more elements such as more than 12 or 14 elements into one nanosystem.. Quote: "The real active sites of high-entropy catalysts for many reactions are still misty, especially for more complicated high-entropy systems such as HEOs/noble metal composites."

card: Paper card. Question: Can machine learning reliably predict the crystal structure (FCC, BCC, FCC+BCC, MIP) of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) synthesized via melting and casting routes without using synthetic data augmentation, and is synthetic data augmentation a reliable practice for this domain?. System: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) comprising 30 elements (Al, Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, Cu, Mn, Ti, V, Nb, Mo, Zr, Hf, Ta, W, C, Mg, Zn, Si, Re, N, Li, Sn, Be, B, Ag, Pt, Y, Pd, Au); specifically a novel alloy Ni25Cu18.75Fe25Co25Al6.25.. Processing: Vacuum arc melting of elemental buttons (Ni, Cu, Fe, Co, Al; purity > 99.99%) under high purity Ar environment, followed by multiple melting/solidification cycles for homogeneity, vacuum sealing in quartz tube, homogenization at 1000 °C for 10 h, and water quenching.. Test conditions: Machine learning models trained on 1200 experimental datasets from melting/casting routes; tested on 240 samples from original data and 279 samples from augmented data (1200 original + 192 synthetic); XRD analysis performed with Cu Kα radiation (λ = 1.54056 Å) at 20°–100° (2θ).. Findings: The vanilla Random Forest Classifier (V-RFC) achieved the highest performance with an average test accuracy of 84%, ROC-AUC score of 0.9649, and tenfold cross-validation mean score of 0.9315.; Synthetic data augmentation using SMOTE-Tomek links increased average test accuracy to 92% (1392 datasets) but did not yield significant breakthroughs in correct/incorrect phase predictions compared to the original dataset.; The V-RFC model correctly predicted the FCC phase for the newly synthesized alloy Ni25Cu18.75Fe25Co25Al6.25, which was confirmed by XRD showing Bragg's peaks (111), (200), (220), (311), and (222).; Five physical parameters (VEC, ∆χ, ∆Smix, δ, ∆Hmix) were identified as crucial for phase prediction, with no strong multicollinearity observed between them.; The model was limited in interpreting the exact number and types of phases in complex multiphase HEAs, often classifying them broadly as MIP (Mixture of Intermetallic Phases).; Hyper-parameter tuning of the RFC model (HT-RFC) resulted in an approximate 3% increment in average test accuracy to 87.49%.; The study found that mixing data from different synthesis routes causes spurious effects, justifying the exclusion of non-melting/casting routes from the dataset.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the Random Forest Classifier's ensemble of decision trees effectively handles the imbalanced dataset of experimental data without the need for synthetic augmentation, which they claim introduces uncertainty regarding whether generated samples are truly high-entropy alloys. The model relies on the correlation of five thermodynamic and geometric parameters (VEC, ∆χ, ∆Smix, δ, ∆Hmix) to distinguish between solid-solution phases (FCC, BCC) and intermetallic mixtures (MIP).. Limitations: The method is limited in exactly interpreting the number and types of phases present in a complex multiphase HEA, as it typically predicts such cases as a single 'MIP' category rather than resolving specific phase combinations.. Future work: A follow-on work will test and predict the mechanical properties of HEAs, which will require atomistic studies using Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations with EAM potentials for 16 elements (Cu, Ag, Au, Ni, Pd, Pt, Al, Pb, Fe, Mo, Ta, W, Mg, Co, Ti, Zr).. Quote: "We found that (i) RFC model predictions were more reliable in contrast to other models and (ii) the synthetic data augmentation is not a neat practice in materials science specially to develop HEAs, where it cannot assure phase information reliably."

Processing: Compilation of data from published reports from 2004 to 2016; density estimated using rule of mixtures (ROM): ρ=∑xiMi/∑xiVi; Young's modulus estimated using ROM for single phase solid solutions only: E=∑xiEi.. Test conditions: Uniaxial loading (tension or compression) at room temperature for 370 alloys; temperature-dependent testing for 27 refractory HEAs (RHEAs).. Findings: The database covers mechanical properties for 370 HEAs and CCAs reported between 2004 and 2016.; For 27 refractory HEAs, yield stress and elongation are provided as a function of testing temperature.; The database includes alloy composition, microstructure type, density, hardness, yield strength, elongation, ultimate strength, and Young's modulus.; Data entries are organized in a tree-like classification with four families and expanded into classes based on principal element combinations.; The database enables users to browse, search, filter, and plot material property maps using performance indices defined by M. F. Ashby.. Mechanism: The authors explain that HEAs are presumably stabilized by the configurational entropy of mixing, while CCAs encompass a broader range of alloys with single-phase or multi-phase microstructures; the database allows for the evaluation of performance indices for lighter, stronger, and stiffer structures.. Future work: The database can be used to represent various property spaces, calculate performance indices, and enable data mining to extract insights and uncover patterns to guide and accelerate the development of HEAs and CCAs.. card: Paper card. Question: How can a comprehensive, updated database of mechanical properties and observed phases for multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) be compiled to aid in identifying design space gaps and training machine learning models?. System: 630 multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs), including complex concentrated alloys (CCAs) with 3 or more principal elements, covering single-phase BCC, single-phase FCC, and multiphase/other microstructures.. Processing: Data extraction from 265 articles (including 136 new articles published in 2019) using keyword search for 'high entropy alloy' on Web of Science; data digitized from plots using webplotdigitizer and combined with previous reviews from 2018.. Test conditions: Mechanical testing performed under tension (T) or compression (C) at various temperatures; properties extracted include yield strength, ultimate tensile/compression strength, elongation, hardness, and Young's modulus.. Findings: The database contains 1545 records from 265 articles, representing a > 100% improvement in available data compared to 2018 reviews.; The study extracted 334 unique MPEA compositions (931 composition-property combinations) in addition to the 296 unique compositions from previous reviews.; Data fields include normalized alloy composition, experimentally observed phases, processing method, grain size, density, and interstitial contents (O, N, C).; Extreme values in property distributions were identified using box plots and investigated for removal or correction.; The database is hosted on Citrination and includes Physical Information File (PIF) records for machine learning applications.; Visualizations of yield strength vs. elongation and temperature dependence of yield strength were generated to guide future research.. Mechanism: The authors explain that the large compositional design space of MPEAs (e.g., 143,000 potential 5-component systems) makes experimental examination of each system prohibitively expensive, necessitating data-driven methods and accurate data accounting to accelerate exploration.. Limitations: Not all properties in the database are reported for every record; specifically, grain size and interstitial contents are missing from many articles despite their importance for refractory MPEAs.. Future work: Researchers are encouraged to contribute new data to the database via a template on GitHub and upload to Citrination to ensure routine updating and improved predictive capabilities for machine learning models.. Question: How to systematically document experimentally reported high-entropy alloy microstructures and metallurgy-specific features to support machine learning-based phase classification?. System: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) comprising 1362 multicomponent alloys selected through the end of August 2020, excluding glassy, amorphous, and hexagonal close-packed phases. Findings: The dataset contains 1422 entries with seventeen columns covering identification, composition, empirical parameters, processing, and microstructure; The final dataset includes 1362 multicomponent alloys after removing entries with missing data and eliminating glassy, amorphous, and hexagonal close-packed phases; Microstructural phases are categorized as single solid solution (FCC, BCC), dual-phase (FCC+BCC), or other intermetallic/laves/martensitic phases (Im); Empirical design parameters calculated include density estimate, enthalpy of mixing (dHmix), entropy of mixing (dSmix), melting temperature (Tm), valence electron concentration (VEC), atomic size difference (δ), and difference in Pauling negativities (χ); Visualization shows that solid solution phases are particularly more sensitive to empirical parameters than intermetallic (IM) phases. Mechanism: The authors explain that the dataset serves as a systematic documentation to enable machine learning and material informatics methods to extract insights and trends not immediately available from individual studies. Limitations: The article is limited to typical empirical parameters for succinctness, though others can be developed from alloy specifications. card: Paper card. Question: Which equimolar quinary combinations of 40 metallic elements form thermodynamically stable single-phase solid solutions, and what are the driving factors (mixing enthalpy, melting point, intermetallic competition) governing their formation?. System: Equimolar quinary alloys from 40 elements (e.g., AlCoMnNiV, CoFeMnNiZn, Cantor alloy CoCrFeMnNi). Processing: High-throughput density-functional theory (DFT) calculations using a binary regular solid-solution model; experimental synthesis via arc-melting (AlCoMnNiV) and mechanical alloying followed by spark plasma sintering (CoFeMnNiZn). Test conditions: Thermodynamic stability assessed at temperatures ranging from 800 to 1600 K, with optimal screening at T = 0.9Tm; experimental validation via SEM, XRD, and EDS after heat treatment at 1373 K (AlCoMnNiV) and 1073–1273 K (CoFeMnNiZn). Findings: Identified 30,201 potential single-phase equimolar alloys out of 658,008 candidates (4.6% of combinations).; 74% of the predicted stable HEAs form in body-centered cubic (BCC) structures.; The model achieved a predictive accuracy of 74% at T = 1350 K, outperforming empirical rules and free-energy models.; High melting point (Tm) is the primary driving factor for HEA formation, with nearly 80% of predicted HEAs containing at least one refractory element.; Al and Zn are outliers that form HEAs easily despite low melting points (933 K and 692 K, respectively) due to favorable mixing with high-melting elements.; The mixing enthalpy of solid solutions correlates linearly with the formation enthalpy of competing intermetallics (IMs).; Successfully synthesized and confirmed the existence of BCC AlCoMnNiV (lattice parameter 2.9 Å) and FCC CoFeMnNiZn (lattice parameter 3.635 Å).; The model predicts that substituting Cr with Zn in the Cantor alloy yields the most stable FCC single-phase HEA among Zn-containing variants.. Mechanism: Phase stability is determined by the competition between the Gibbs free energy of the solid solution (driven by configurational entropy and mixing enthalpy) and the free energy of competing intermetallic phases. High melting points allow for high synthesis temperatures where entropic stabilization dominates, while mild mixing enthalpy often correlates with weak intermetallic competition, facilitating solid solution formation.. Limitations: The model does not account for vibrational entropy, magnetic ordering, or short-range ordering, which would increase computational cost; it also struggles to discriminate between HCP and FCC structures due to their small energy difference.. Future work: Future screenings can incorporate vibrational effects, magnetic ordering, and short-range ordering in a tiered approach; the model can be applied to non-equimolar compositions and tailored for specific properties beyond phase stability.. Quote: "We identify 30,201 potential single-phase equimolar alloys (5% of the possible combinations) forming mainly in body-centered cubic structures."

Mechanism: The authors employed an in-house thermodynamic database combined with a parametric criterion to generate binary priority lists, enabling the rapid screening of multicomponent alloys for single-phase solid solution formation..
