card: Paper card. Question: How can high-entropy alloys be recommended effectively when existing data is limited, biased, and lacks sufficient descriptors for alloys with varying numbers of components?. System: Equiatomic alloys comprising elements from the set {Fe, Co, Ir, Cu, Ni, Pt, Pd, Rh, Au, Ag, Ru, Os, Si, As, Al, Tc, Re, Mn, Ta, Ti, W, Mo, Cr, V, Hf, Nb, Zr}, specifically focusing on Fe-Co-based quaternary alloys (FeMnCoNi) and early transition metal alloys.. Processing: Development of an evidence-based recommender system (ERS) using Dempster–Shafer theory to model, collect, and combine pieces of evidence from existing datasets without using material descriptors; experimental validation involved synthesizing Fe0.25Co0.25Mn0.25Ni0.25 thin films annealed at 400 °C.. Test conditions: Evaluation performed via k-fold cross-validation on four datasets (ASMI16, CALPHAD, AFLOW, LTVC) containing binary, ternary, quaternary, and quinary alloys; extrapolation tests conducted on quaternary and quinary HEAs; experimental validation on thin films annealed at 400 °C.. Findings: The ERS outperforms matrix-factorization (NMF, SVD) and supervised-learning (SVM, logistic regression, decision tree, naive Bayes) systems in k-fold cross-validation across all four datasets.; The ERS demonstrates superior extrapolation capabilities, requiring approximately 10–100 fewer trials to recall 50% and 75% of quinary HEAs compared to NMF and SVD systems.; Supervised-learning methods failed to rank HEAs effectively in datasets containing only positively labeled HEAs, performing either randomly or failing to rank any.; The ERS identified FeCoMnNi as the only Fe-Mn-Co-based quaternary candidate with a belief higher than 0.5.; Experimental validation confirmed that the Fe0.25Co0.25Mn0.25Ni0.25 thin film annealed at 400 °C exhibits a body-centered cubic (BCC) structure, evidenced by a reflection at 2θ = 44.7°.; Similarity analysis revealed three distinct element groups corresponding to early transition metals, late transition metals, and a third group with no evidence of similarity in the ASMI16 dataset.; Elements with the same periodic table group index (Δgroup = 0) showed high similarity scores, while similarity decreased as Δgroup increased to 3 or 4.; In the absence of sufficient evidence for mixtures of many elements, the system retained a large degree of uncertainty, with m({HEA, ¬HEA}) ≈ 1.. Mechanism: The ERS uses the elemental substitution method where pairs of observed alloys serve as evidence to measure substitutability between element combinations; Dempster–Shafer theory assigns mass functions to subsets of a frame of discernment ({similar, dissimilar} or {HEA, ¬HEA}) to model uncertainty, combining multiple pieces of evidence using the Dempster rule to rank potential alloys without relying on material descriptors.. Limitations: The system does not answer essential questions regarding the specific crystal structure or other properties of the HEAs beyond phase existence; detailed quantitative investigation of secondary phases in the synthesized FeCoMnNi alloy thin film was not done due to technical difficulties; the system cannot reliably recall the remaining one-quarter of HEAs in some datasets due to insufficient evidence in the training data.. Future work: The authors propose that by redesigning the frame of discernment to reflect additional properties of interest, the model can be constructed to recommend potential alloys forming HEA phases with desirable properties beyond just phase existence.. Quote: "To overcome these issues, here we show the development of an evidence-based material recommender system (ERS) that adopts Dempster–Shafer theory, a general framework for reasoning with uncertainty."

Paper card. Question: How can a recommender system be constructed to identify unknown High-Entropy Alloy (HEA) compositions and extrapolate recommendations to higher-order alloys (quaternary and quinary) based on binary and ternary training data?. System: Alloys composed of 27 elements; specific datasets include D_AFLOW (binary/ternary), D_LTVC (binary/ternary), D_ASMI16 (binary), D_CALPHAD (ternary); case study: Fe0.25Co0.25Mn0.25Ni0.25 thin films. Processing: Machine learning: Grid search for hyperparameter α (0.01 to 0.9); Ninefold cross-validation repeated 100 times; Experimental: Combinatorial multitarget radio frequency sputtering (100 W FeCoMn, 120 W Ni) at 0.3 Pa Ar, deposition rate 0.23 ± 0.01 nm s–1, annealing at 400 °C for 30 min under vacuum < 6 × 10−3 Pa. Test conditions: Cross-validation on D_AFLOW (80% accuracy), D_LTVC (75% accuracy), D_ASMI16 (40/45 training, 5/45 test), D_CALPHAD (216/243 training, 27/243 test); Extrapolation to 17,550 quaternary and 80,730 quinary alloys; Thin film characterization via XRD and XRF. Findings: Cross-validated testing accuracy rates were 80% for D_AFLOW and 75% for D_LTVC.; The absolute value of alpha (α) has little effect on the final result of the recommender system.; A total of 351 hypothetical binary alloys were generated from 27 elements, with 45 in the training set and 306 ranked by the model.; For ternary alloys, 2,925 hypothetical combinations were generated from 27 elements, with 243 in the training set and 2,682 ranked.; The model ranked 17,550 quaternary alloys and 80,730 quinary alloys for synthesis candidates.; The BCC phase was confirmed for the annealed thin film sample at the equiatomic composition of FeCoMnNi.; Phase separation and inflection points were observed near 400 °C for FeCoMn-X compositions.. Mechanism: The system uses a rating matrix representation where alloys are decomposed into elementary components (A and B) to build a user-item matrix. It learns a similarity matrix between elements (and binary combinations) from training data to predict ratings for missing elements, allowing the ranking of hypothetical alloys. The method accounts for uncertainty by adding a degree of uncertainty α in the mass function.. Limitations: The compositional descriptor cannot be applied in the case of having extrapolation in the number of components. The experiments do not use the selected alloys (test set) to improve the accuracy of the model for the next trial due to computational cost.. Future work: Structural changes at higher temperatures for FeCoMnNi are expected and are currently under investigation.. Quote: "The compositional descriptor therefore cannot be applied in the case of having extrapolation in the number of components."

card: Paper card. Question: How can single-phase refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) be designed to achieve ultrahigh yield strength at 1600°C, and what is the underlying deformation mechanism responsible for the observed plateau strength?. System: Hf0.5MoNbTaW and HfMoNbTaW refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs). Processing: Vacuum arc melting followed by homogenization treatment at 2100°C for 2 hours with subsequent air cooling in an ultrahigh-temperature furnace under Ar flow. Test conditions: Compression testing at a strain rate of 10⁻³ 1/s from ambient temperature to 1600°C; samples were 3.6 mm in diameter and 6 mm in height for 1600°C tests. Findings: HfMoNbTaW alloy after homogenization exhibits a yield strength of 571 MPa at 1600°C, which is higher than MoNbTaVW (477 MPa).; A plateau of strength occurs from 800°C to 1200°C for HfMoNbTaW, with a value of approximately 950 MPa.; Homogenization at 2100°C for 2 h results in a homogeneous body-centered cubic (bcc) phase with no precipitation.; The theoretical yield strength (σycal) for HfMoNbTaW increases by 30.8% from 2393 MPa to 3131 MPa upon equiatomic addition of Hf into MoNbTaW.; The shear modulus of HfMoNbTaW was measured to be 73 ± 1 GPa via nanoindentation.; Extrapolation of high-temperature strength data suggests a room temperature strength of 4536 MPa, consistent with edge dislocation control calculations (4206 MPa).; Adding Hf to MoNbTaW increases yield strength by 47.5% compared to MoNbTaW (1561 MPa vs 1058 MPa).. Mechanism: The authors propose that the plateau strength and ultrahigh elevated-temperature strength result from a transition in the deformation mode from screw dislocations to edge dislocations. Below the critical temperature (Tc), strength decreases due to thermal activation of screw dislocations. Above Tc, edge dislocations become dominant in general yielding, leading to a plateau in strength and high strength at elevated temperatures.. Limitations: The text notes that the theoretical yield strength calculated using the average shear modulus (Gmix) is generally larger than the experimental value, and that the assumption of mixed dislocation control (α=9) was an overestimate compared to screw dislocation control (α=2) at low temperatures.. Future work: The authors state that a similar alloy design strategy could be applied to develop more RHEAs with an ultrahigh strength level.. Quote: "HfMoNbTaW alloy exhibits a yield strength of 571 MPa at 1600°C, much higher than that of MoNbTaVW (477 MPa)."

card: Paper card. Question: How to achieve a simultaneous balance of high fracture strength and high ductility in high-entropy alloys while overcoming inferior castability and compositional segregation?. System: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA). Processing: Vacuum induction melting of commercially pure elements (Al, Co, Ni: 99.9 wt.%; Cr, Fe: 99.5 ~ 99.6 wt.%) in a BN crucible; heating to 600°C for 1 hour; pouring at 1500°C into a MgO crucible (220 mm length, 62 mm upper ID, 50 mm bottom ID) under argon atmosphere (0.06 MPa); bulk ingot weight ~2.5 kg.. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile tests at strain rate 1 × 10−3 s−1; elevated temperature tests at 600°C and 700°C at strain rate 1 × 10−3 s−1; cold rolling with 8% thickness reduction followed by tensile testing at 2 × 10−3 s−1.. Findings: The as-cast alloy exhibited a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure with an inter-lamellar spacing of about 2 μm.; Room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6%.; The proof stress was 75 MPa, while the fracture stress reached close to 1.2 GPa (true stress condition).; At 600°C, the alloy maintained a fracture stress of 806 MPa and elongation of 33.7%.; At 700°C, the alloy maintained a fracture stress of 538 MPa and elongation of 22.9%.; Cold rolling with 8% reduction increased the true fracture stress to 1265 MPa while maintaining 9.9% elongation.; The density of the EHEA was measured to be 7.38 g/cm3.; The ratio of fracture strength to proof stress (σUTS/σ0.2) was close to 16.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the unprecedented strain hardening and balanced properties to the fine regular lamellar structure that easily stores dislocations and the alternating soft fcc phases and hard B2-structured NiAl-rich phases. When dislocations pass through soft fcc phases, the hard B2 phases, including nanoscale precipitates, pin the movement of dislocations resulting in significant work hardening.. Limitations: The text notes that the mechanism for the low elastic limit (proof stress) is still unclear at this stage.. Future work: Further exploration of new EHEAs will be based on physical metallurgy principles using atomic radius, mixing enthalpy, and valence electron concentration; thermodynamics calculations based on the CALPHAD method can provide guidance once reliable databases are established; the potential for producing ultrahigh strength components after large plastic deformation awaits further investigations.. Quote: "To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases."

card: Paper card. Question: What are the individual effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on the microstructure and mechanical properties (yield strength, ductility, and elevated-temperature performance) of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr refractory high-entropy alloys?. System: Equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr and its five sub-alloys created by the subtraction method: HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi. Processing: Vacuum-arc melting of 99.9 wt.% (99.99 wt.% for Ti) pure elements stacked by melting point, re-melted at least four times, and solidified in a water-cool copper mold. Test conditions: Compression tests at room temperature, 800 °C, 1000 °C, 1200 °C, and 1400 °C; crosshead speed 0.36 mm/min (strain rate 10⁻³ s⁻¹); cylindrical samples 3.6 mm diameter x 6 mm height. Findings: HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy yield strength was 1512 MPa at room temperature and 556 MPa at 1200 °C.; HfMoTaTiZr (Nb removed) showed the highest room temperature yield strength of 1600 MPa but lower toughness.; HfMoNbTaTi (Zr removed) exhibited the best comprehensive properties with 27% fracture strain at room temperature and 367 MPa yield strength at 1400 °C.; The presence of Mo increased room temperature yield strength from 929 MPa (in HfNbTaTiZr) to 1512 MPa but reduced fracture strain from >50% to 12%.; Nb addition increased yield strength by 38% at 1200 °C and significantly improved room temperature fracture strain.; Zr addition increased strength but strongly deteriorated room temperature toughness, reducing fracture strain from 27% to 12%.; Alloys with Mo present showed much better strength at elevated temperatures compared to HfNbTaTiZr.; At 1200 °C, HfMoNbTaTi alloy had the highest specific strength among the tested alloys.. Mechanism: The high yield strength is attributed to the solid solution strengthening effect driven by atomic size and shear modulus mismatch; the high entropy effect promotes the formation of a single BCC disordered solid solution phase despite binary phase diagrams suggesting intermetallics; severe lattice distortion reduces the effective shear modulus by approximately 30% compared to the rule of mixtures.. Limitations: There is a deviation of about 30% between calculated and experimental yield strengths, likely due to overestimated shear modulus; the criteria for Laves phase formation were not fully consistent with experimental observations; the reduction in shear modulus due to lattice distortion requires further research to confirm reasons.. Future work: Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are required for high-temperature applications in air; more research is needed to confirm the elemental effects in other RHEA systems and to understand the reasons for reduced shear modulus.. Quote: "The subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element"

card: Paper card. Question: How does a novel refractory high entropy alloy (NV1) behave under long-term isothermal oxidation at 1000 °C and 1100 °C, and what is the mechanism governing its oxidation resistance over 200 hours?. System: NV1 alloy (Al, Cr, Mo, Nb, Si, Ta, Ti; designed based on CrMo0.5NbTa0.5TiZr with reduced Ti, removed Zr, and added Al, Si, increased Cr). Processing: Cold crucible levitation melting of high purity elemental raw materials (>99.9 wt%) to cast a 1.1 kg cone-shaped ingot; samples machined by electrical discharge machining and ground to 1200 grit; isothermal oxidation performed in flowing dry air using a thermogravimetric analyser (SETARAM TAG 24-18S) and muffle furnace. Test conditions: Isothermal oxidation at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours in flowing dry air; microstructural characterization performed at intervals of 1, 12, 40, 50, 100, and 200 hours. Findings: At 1000 °C, the mass gain after 200 hours was 6.53 mg/cm2, following an exponential dependence throughout the entire duration.; At 1100 °C, the mass gain after 200 hours was 4.03 mg/cm2, which is lower than at 1000 °C, showing three stages of parabolic dependence.; The external oxide layer at both temperatures consisted primarily of a CrTaO4-based oxide with dispersed Al2O3 and Cr2O3.; At 1000 °C, the CrTaO4-based oxide layer was porous with large volume defects due to insufficient kinetics, preventing it from acting as an effective barrier.; At 1100 °C, the CrTaO4-based oxide layer was denser and more continuous, leading to controlled oxidation and reduced weight gain.; TiN particles (size ~1.5 μm) formed preferentially within the Mo-rich dendritic regions at both temperatures, while Al2O3 formed in the internal oxidation depth.; The CrTaO4-based oxide at 1100 °C contained up to 7 at% Al and 2.2 at% less Cr compared to the oxide formed at 1000 °C, indicating non-stoichiometric substitution.. Mechanism: At 1000 °C, insufficient kinetics prevented the formation of a dense, protective CrTaO4 layer, leading to heterogeneous oxidation, volume defects, and exponential weight gain driven by external oxidation and nitridation. At 1100 °C, enhanced diffusion kinetics allowed for the homogeneous growth of a denser, continuous CrTaO4-based layer that acted as a barrier to oxygen and element diffusion, resulting in parabolic weight gain; however, Mo evaporation at the oxide/substrate interface in Stage II temporarily accelerated oxidation before Stage III saw further CrTaO4 formation.. Limitations: The study notes that while CrTaO4-based oxide provided protection, it could not fully prevent the ingestion of oxygen and nitrogen, leading to internal oxidation and nitridation over the long duration.. Future work: The authors propose that the nature of the CrTaO4-based oxide needs to be carefully examined in future studies, and that the influence of nitridation on RHEA properties is an important subject for further investigation.. Quote: "At 1100 °C, mass gain curve showed two parabolic dependences associated with the formation of protective CrTaO4-based oxide layer and the weight gain after 200 hours was 4.03 mg/cm2"

card: Paper card. Question: How does the addition of 0.71 wt.% Zr affect the microstructure, elastic modulus, and corrosion resistance of a CoCrFeMoNi high-entropy alloy designed for geothermal applications?. System: CoCrFeMoNi (Sample 1) and CoCrFeMoNi + 0.71 wt.% Zr (Sample 2). Processing: Vacuum arc remelting (VAR) using MRF ABJ 900 VAR equipment under argon atmosphere with six remelting operations for homogenization; samples ground and polished to mirror finish with 0.1 µm alumina suspension. Test conditions: Three-point bending test (ISO 7438:2020) for Young's modulus; microhardness test (1.96 N load, ISO 14577-1:2015); electrochemical tests in 3.5% NaCl solution at room temperature including linear polarization (±25 mV vs Ecorr, 0.166 mV/s sweep), potentiodynamic polarization (-1.2 to +1.2 V vs SCE), and EIS (10⁻¹ to 10⁵ Hz). Findings: The Young's modulus of the Zr-free alloy (Sample 1) was 20.5% higher than that of the Zr-doped alloy (Sample 2).; The addition of Zr increased the average microhardness of the high-entropy alloy.; The corrosion rate increased from 2.44 × 10⁻³ mmpy for Sample 1 to 2.80 × 10⁻³ mmpy for Sample 2, representing a ~16-fold increase compared to Sample 1.; The polarization resistance (R2) of the passive film decreased from 2.57 × 10⁷ kΩ·cm² for Sample 1 to 1.47 × 10⁵ kΩ·cm² for Sample 2.; The addition of Zr caused grain refinement and reduced the volume fraction of interdendritic zones.; The tendency to form the sigma phase was diminished in Sample 2 due to a decrease in Mo concentration in interdendritic zones from 20 at.% to 17 at.%.; Both alloys exhibited brittle fracture with cleavage-like fracture planes.. Mechanism: The decrease in corrosion resistance and passive film resistance with Zr addition is attributed to the formation of a thicker but more defective passive film containing an increased number of defective spots, potentially involving the in situ formation of ZrO2 which explains the high corrosion rate. The grain refinement and hardness increase are due to Zr obstructing grain coarsening and creating a supersaturated solid solution.. W2883475578.title: Enhanced strength and ductility of a tungsten-doped CoCrNi medium-entropy alloy

card: Paper card. Question: How does varying the nickel atomic ratio (x = 1.0, 1.4, 1.8) in the AlCrFeCoNi system affect the microstructure, microhardness, and corrosion behavior in simulated body fluids?. System: AlCrFeCoNix alloys with x = 1.0, 1.4, and 1.8. Processing: Vacuum Arc Remelting (VAR) using high purity raw materials (≥99.5%), followed by flipping and re-melting 6 times under Argon; homogenization via annealing at 1100 °C for 48 h followed by water quenching. Test conditions: Immersion in Ringer Grifols solution at 37 ± 0.1 °C for one week; potentiodynamic polarization from -800 mV to +500 mV vs SCE at 1 mV/s; Vickers microhardness with 100 g load for 15 s. Findings: Hardness values decreased from 562 HV for AlCrFeCoNi to 455 HV for AlCrFeCoNi1.4 and 316 HV for AlCrFeCoNi1.8.; The pitting potential (Enp) increased with nickel content: 185 mV for x=1.0, 245 mV for x=1.4, and 385 mV for x=1.8.; Al concentration in the surface region dropped from ~10 at% to 2.57–3.03 at% after heat treatment and corrosion.; Open circuit potential increased by 30–50 mV during the first 24 hours due to passive layer growth.; The extent of interdendritic areas increased with nickel concentration, with Cr more segregated in interdendritic areas than in dendrites.; Corrosion current densities were much lower than those of 304SS, indicating higher resistance to general corrosion.. Mechanism: The decrease in hardness is attributed to the dissolution of Cr and Fe precipitates in the nickel-rich matrix, forming a continuous solid solution. The improved corrosion resistance with higher Ni content is linked to a more positive pit nucleation potential and a larger difference between nucleation and repassivation potentials, suggesting a strong tendency for pit repassivation. The formation of an Al-Ni compound after thermal treatment is hypothesized to corrode faster than the main HEA phase, leading to the observed drop in Al and Ni concentrations on the surface.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study, though it notes that Ni content is not the only factor affecting corrosion, as microstructure and element distribution also play roles.. Future work: The authors propose that by manipulating the composition and structure of HEAs, their mechanical and chemical performance could be optimized to meet the requirements for their usage as novel medical instruments materials.. Quote: "Hardness values decreased as the percentage of nickel increased due to the dissolution of the precipitates in a nickel-rich matrix and consequently the formation of continuous solid solutions."

W3012033042.title: Microstructure and mechanical properties of CoCrFeNiMo high-entropy alloy coatings

card: Paper card. Question: How can the deformation mechanisms (TRIP vs. TWIP) in face-centered cubic high-entropy alloys be accurately predicted to overcome the strength-ductility trade-off, given the limitations of the intrinsic stacking fault energy (ISFE) criterion?. System: Co-Cr-Fe-Mn-Ni high-entropy alloys (specifically CoxCr44-xFe26Mn10Ni8 and Co36CrxFe46-xMn10Ni8 series) and literature-reported TRIP/TWIP steels. Processing: Arc melting of high-purity elements followed by homogenization at 1200°C for 1 hour and water quenching; cold rolling with 60% thickness reduction; uniaxial compression at 20% strain with a strain rate of 10⁻³ s⁻¹. Test conditions: Room temperature (293 K) for thermodynamic calculations; microstructure characterized via EBSD and HRTEM after deformation; hardness measured using Vickers microhardness tester (100 gram-force, 10-s dwelling time). Findings: The traditional ISFE criterion fails to predict deformation mechanisms in more than 50% of the studied cases, with an accuracy of only about 56%.; The proposed UMFE/UTFE criterion accurately predicts the deformation mechanisms (TRIP vs. TWIP) in all 7 designed HEAs and tested steels, achieving 100% accuracy.; Seven new HEAs were successfully designed and experimentally verified to exhibit either TRIP or TWIP behavior based on the UMFE < UTFE or UMFE > UTFE criteria.; Co content increases the energy barrier for stacking fault and twin formation (USFE and UTFE) but decreases ISFE, UMFE, and ME energy.; Ni content exhibits a strong effect on increasing ISFE, ESFE/TEE, UMFE, and MEE, limiting its content to promote the TRIP effect.; TRIP-dominant alloys show higher hardness compared to TWIP-dominant alloys, with hardness increasing after deformation due to high-strain hardening.; In TWIP steels, the calculated ISFE was -289.2 mJ/m², making it impossible to predict the mechanism, whereas UTFE (107.3 mJ/m²) was much smaller than UMFE (243.6 mJ/m²), correctly indicating twinning dominance.. Mechanism: The competition between martensitic transformation and twinning is governed by the energy barriers defined by the difference between unstable fault energies and ISFE (UMFE-ISFE and UTFE-ISFE). Martensitic transformation prevails when the unstable martensite fault energy (UMFE) is smaller than the unstable twin fault energy (UTFE), while deformation twinning dominates if UMFE is larger than UTFE. These unstable fault energies represent the energy barriers for the formation of martensite and twin embryos, respectively, which ISFE does not capture.. Limitations: The study did not test tensile properties, which are more appropriate to evaluate the mechanical properties of the designed HEAs. Discrepancies between CALPHAD-based thermodynamic models and DFT calculations regarding fcc stability exist and could be reduced by more advanced models considering interfacial energy.. Future work: To perform systematic mechanical property evaluation, specifically tensile testing, to select the best HEAs with potential applications and to accelerate the discovery of TRIP/TWIP in a wide spectrum of alloys using the proposed design paradigm.. Quote: "Among the studied HEAs and steels, the traditional ISFE criterion fails in more than half of the cases, while the UMFE/UTFE criterion accurately predicts the deformation mechanisms in all cases."

card: Paper card. Question: What is the influence of the nanocrystalline structure produced by severe plastic deformation (SPD) on the corrosion behavior of CoCrFeMnNi alloys with varying Cr contents?. System: CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloys with Cr contents ranging from 0 to 20 at.% (Co, Fe, Mn, Ni adjusted to be equiatomic, 20 to 25 at.%). Processing: Arc melting followed by homogenization annealing at 1273 K for 16 h (repeated four times); High-Pressure Torsion (HPT) at room temperature with a pressure of 6.0 GPa at 1 rpm for 10 turns. Test conditions: Potentiodynamic polarization in 0.5 M H2SO4 and 3.5 wt.% NaCl solutions at room temperature; scan rate of 20 mV/min; samples immersed for 1 hour prior to testing; dissolved oxygen removed with argon gas. Findings: Hardness increased significantly by a factor of 4 to Hv = 510 after HPT processing compared to the initial hardness of Hv = 120.; The average grain size of HPT samples was about 40 nm with high-angle grain boundaries.; Polarization curves for HPT and coarse-grained (CG) samples almost completely overlapped in 0.5 M H2SO4, indicating nanocrystalline formation did not alter electrochemical behavior.; In 3.5% NaCl, passive currents for HPT samples stayed constant until breakdown potential, while CG samples showed gradually increasing currents.; Critical pitting potential (Epit) increased with Cr content in both CG and HPT specimens, but little difference was observed between HPT and CG samples.; Cr enrichment levels in passivation films (Cr/(Fe + Cr + Co + Ni + Mn) ratio) were comparable in both CG and UFG specimens and smaller than 0.5.; Cr was the dominant element providing passivation ability, with passive current decreasing as Cr content increased.. Mechanism: The negligible impact of grain refinement on corrosion is attributed to high-entropy effects: the high-entropy effect suppresses selective dissolution of specific elements, and sluggish diffusion prevents Cr from diffusing from the base metal to the passivation film through high-density grain boundaries, unlike in binary Fe-Cr alloys.. Limitations: The text states that the raw processed data required to reproduce the findings cannot be shared as they form part of an ongoing study; it also notes that the reason for inconsistency with previous HPT hardness results is unknown.. Quote: "The impact of the nanocrystalline structure produced by SPD on the corrosion behavior was negligibly small."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the microstructure and phase stability of an equiatomic CrNiCoFeMn high-entropy alloy evolve during and after selective laser melting (SLM) and subsequent high-temperature annealing, and what is the impact on mechanical properties?. System: Equiatomic CrNiCoFeMn (Cantor alloy) produced from mechanically alloyed powders (purity >97 at.%). Processing: Selective Laser Melting (SLM) using SISMA MYSINT100 RM with Nitrogen atmosphere (O2 <0.5%), layer thickness H=0.05 mm, energy density F=200 J/mm3, recoating rate 70/150 mm/s, spot diameter 50 μm; followed by cold rolling (90% thickness reduction) and annealing at 723–1423 K for 25 h or 1170 K for 100 h. Test conditions: Microstructural analysis via XRD, SEM-FEG-EDS, and EBSD; mechanical testing via Vickers microhardness; annealing temperatures: 723, 823, 923, 1023, 1123, 1223, 1323, 1423 K. Findings: The as-built SLM alloy contains fine Cr-rich nitride and σ phase precipitates despite XRD showing a single FCC structure.; Precipitates increase in number and size after annealing between 900 K and 1300 K, with σ phase nucleating at grain boundaries and triple points.; At 1423 K, the σ phase and most nitrides dissolve, resulting in a single FCC structure with near-equieatomic composition.; Cold rolling followed by annealing accelerates recrystallization and σ phase precipitation compared to as-built samples.; Microhardness increases significantly after cold rolling and at low annealing temperatures (723–823 K) due to fine precipitates.; Hardness decreases progressively above 1023 K as σ phase grows and grains coarsen, following the Hall–Petch relationship.; The σ phase is tetragonal, Cr-rich (~50 at.%), and forms preferentially at grain boundaries and triple points during recrystallization.. Mechanism: Nitrogen interstitial diffusion during SLM leads to supersaturation and nitride nucleation; subsequent thermal cycles and rapid cooling promote heterogeneous nucleation of σ phase around nitrides. Recrystallization and increased diffusion rates at higher temperatures cause σ phase growth at boundaries, while very high temperatures (≥1423 K) enable dissolution back to a single FCC phase.. Limitations: The text states that distinguishing between Cr2N and CrN via EDS is difficult due to small precipitate size, and that the exact activation energy for precipitation requires further nucleation and coarsening studies.. Future work: Further experimental work focusing on nucleation and coarsening is required to fully understand the precipitation process; thermodynamic databases and models need to be extended to better understand this complex alloy behavior.. Quote: "The as-produced alloy shows fine nitride and σ phase precipitates, which are Cr-rich and stable up to about 900 K."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the addition of 5 at. % Zr to a CoCrFeMnNi Cantor High Entropy Alloy affect its melting temperature, microstructure evolution during recrystallization, and mechanical properties when processed via vacuum induction melting of pre-alloyed powders?. System: Co20Cr20Fe20Mn20Ni20 (base) and Co19Cr19Fe19Mn19Ni19Zr5 (Zr-modified). Processing: Mechanical alloying of elemental powders for 45 h at 400 rpm; vacuum induction melting at >1720 K for 30 min; cold rolling to 90% thickness reduction; annealing at 1143 K (Zr-modified) or 1043 K (base) for 30 min. Test conditions: XRD (35°–100° 2Θ); SEM-EDS; TEM (200 kV); micro-hardness (300 mN and 50 mN loads); mechanical spectroscopy (400–900 Hz, room temp to 700 K at 1.5 K/min). Findings: The Zr-modified alloy exhibits a lower melting temperature due to eutectic formation, with liquid phase formation at about 1470 K compared to 2500 K for traditional arc melting.; The recrystallization temperature of the Zr-modified alloy (1143 K) is higher than that of the base alloy (1043 K).; After recrystallization, the Zr-modified alloy shows an average grain size of (6.0 ± 1.5) μm in dendritic regions and (1.5 ± 0.5) μm in inter-dendritic regions, compared to (15 ± 2) μm for the base alloy.; The Zr-modified alloy contains a coherent second phase (inter-dendritic) with an FCC structure, which is Ni-enriched and Zr-concentrated.; Micro-hardness of the Zr-rich inter-dendritic phase is higher than the dendritic region in as-cast and cold-rolled states, but both phases converge to similar values after recrystallization.; The dynamic Young's modulus at 300 K is (130 ± 10) GPa for the Zr-modified alloy versus (140 ± 10) GPa for the base alloy.; No cracks were observed in the Zr-modified alloy after cold rolling, indicating no significant embrittlement despite Zr addition.; Both alloys maintain an FCC crystallographic structure after annealing, with lattice parameters of (0.358 ± 0.002) nm for the Zr-modified alloy and (0.359 ± 0.002) nm for the base alloy.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the strengthening and grain refinement to the precipitation of a coherent second phase and the influence of Zr solute atoms on recovery and recrystallization processes. Solute atoms impede dislocation climb and cross-slip, leading to finer grains. The coherent nature of the second phase boundaries minimizes impediment to dislocation glide, preserving ductility while enhancing strength through precipitation and lattice distortion.. Limitations: The authors state that a more thorough investigation was not possible due to the limited amount of available material.. Future work: The authors propose that a more thorough investigation will be performed subsequently.. Quote: "A measure of 5 at. % Zr was added, resulting in a liquid phase formation at about 1470 K [,,], to be compared with the 2500 K of a traditional arc melting process."
